\section[autorizar]{autorizar — to authorise, to allow}

\label{lesson:ES-C624-autorizar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to penalise, then the Spanish for to fine.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: autorizar}
\textbf{autorizar} — \textquotedblleft{}to authorise, to allow\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El director autorizó la salida al museo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The head teacher authorised the trip to the museum.}
\end{quote}

Spelling: \emph{autoricé}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{autorizar} is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin \emph{auctorizare}, built on \emph{auctor} 'originator, guarantor', from \emph{augere} 'to increase' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{autorizar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{autorizar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{autorizar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to penalise, then the Spanish for to fine, then say \emph{autorizar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does autorizar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To authorise, to allow\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la autorización]{la autorización — the authorisation, the permission}

\label{lesson:ES-C624-autorizacion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to fine, then the Spanish for to authorise.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la autorización}
\textbf{la autorización} — \textquotedblleft{}the authorisation, the permission\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Necesitas una autorización de tus padres.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{You need your parents' permission.}
\end{quote}

More formal than \emph{el permiso}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{autorización} is built on \emph{autorizar}, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin \emph{auctorizare}, built on \emph{auctor} 'guarantor' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[tramitar]{tramitar — to process, to deal with (paperwork)}

\label{lesson:ES-C624-tramitar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to authorise, then the Spanish for the authorisation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tramitar}
\textbf{tramitar} — \textquotedblleft{}to process, to deal with (paperwork)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tardan un mes en tramitar el permiso.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It takes them a month to process the permit.}
\end{quote}

Formal, for official paperwork.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tramitar} is built on \emph{trámite}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{trames, tramitis} 'a path, a way across' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[el certificado]{el certificado — the certificate}

\label{lesson:ES-C624-certificado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the authorisation, then the Spanish for to process.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el certificado}
\textbf{el certificado} — \textquotedblleft{}the certificate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Necesito un certificado médico.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I need a medical certificate.}
\end{quote}

The verb is \emph{certificar} — to certify.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{certificado} is the participle of \emph{certificar}, which EtymDB traces to Late Latin \emph{certificāre} 'to make sure', built on \emph{certus} 'sure'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[oficial]{oficial — official; the officer}

\label{lesson:ES-C624-oficial}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to process, then the Spanish for the certificate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: oficial}
\textbf{oficial} — \textquotedblleft{}official; the officer\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Es el documento oficial.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is the official document.}
\end{quote}

As a noun it is a rank in the army or the police.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{oficial} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{officialis} 'of duty', built on \emph{officium} 'service, duty' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
